summary.one_sentence: Tulu 3 is an open post-training recipe that combines data curation, SFT, length-normalized DPO, RL with verifiable rewards, decontamination, and staged evaluation.
summary.thesis: The paper's contribution is not just a model checkpoint; it is a transparent pipeline showing how modern open instruction models are built and debugged across data, algorithms, infrastructure, and evaluations.
summary.why_it_matters: For agent training, Tulu 3 is the bridge from RLHF/DPO to verifiable-reward training: it shows how to use exact checks for math and instruction-following, while documenting the operational costs and failure modes of doing that at scale.

prior_state: Open post-training recipes lagged proprietary labs in transparency, scale, and model quality.
Instruction tuning, preference tuning, evaluation, decontamination, and RL were often reported as fragments rather than a reproducible stack.
Open models could overfit popular benchmarks or lack clear unseen evaluations for core capabilities.
Verifiable-reward training was promising but under-documented as a practical post-training stage.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks how to build a fully open, competitive post-training pipeline with released data, code, checkpoints, evaluation tooling, and recipe decisions.
assumptions: Llama 3.1 base models are strong enough bases for competitive open post-training.
A core-skill evaluation suite can guide data and method choices without fully overfitting to development tasks.
Synthetic and public datasets can be curated and decontaminated enough for useful open recipes.
Some target skills have deterministic verifiers suitable for RLVR.

concepts.name: Post-training recipe
concepts.definition: The staged process of data curation, SFT, preference tuning, RLVR, evaluation, and infrastructure choices used to adapt a base model.

concepts.name: Tulu 3 Data
concepts.definition: The released collection of prompt-completion, preference, and verifiable-reward datasets targeting core skills.

concepts.name: Tulu 3 Eval
concepts.definition: A development and unseen evaluation suite covering knowledge, reasoning, math, coding, instruction following, chat, and safety.

concepts.name: Length-normalized DPO
concepts.definition: The DPO variant the paper reports as the best preference tuning choice in its ablations.

concepts.name: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
concepts.definition: A PPO-based stage where completions receive a positive reward only when a deterministic verifier judges the answer correct.

method.core_idea: Build a staged open recipe: curate and decontaminate data around core skills, train SFT checkpoints, generate on-policy preference data and tune with length-normalized DPO, then run PPO with binary verifiable rewards for math and precise instruction-following before validating on development and unseen evaluations.
action_grammar: curate prompts: assemble public and synthetic prompts for target skills.
decontaminate: remove benchmark overlap from open data.
preference generation: compare Tulu 3 SFT completions with outputs from other models.
DPO-norm: tune from preference pairs using length-normalized DPO.
verifier: deterministic correctness function over prompt and completion.
RLVR: sample completions, apply verifier reward, and optimize with PPO.
eval gate: measure development and unseen tasks for each core skill.
steps: Identify core skills: knowledge recall, reasoning, math, coding, chat, safety, and precise instruction following.
Build development and unseen evaluation suites before finalizing recipes.
Curate public and synthetic instruction data and aggressively decontaminate against evaluations.
Train SFT checkpoints on Llama 3.1 base models.
Create on-policy preference data and train DPO checkpoints, selecting length-normalized DPO after ablations.
Train final 8B and 70B models with RLVR using GSM8K, MATH, and IFEval-style verifiers.
Scale the recipe to a 405B model with adjusted SFT/DPO/RLVR details.
Release weights, intermediate checkpoints, datasets, training code, evaluation code, and decontamination tooling.
method.pseudocode:
base = load_llama31(size)

evals = build_eval_suite(dev_tasks, unseen_tasks)
data = decontaminate(curate_public_and_synthetic_data(), evals)

sft = train_sft(base, data.sft_mix, loss="sum", epochs=2)
prefs = generate_on_policy_preferences(sft, data.preference_prompts)
dpo = train_dpo_norm(sft, prefs)

for prompt in data.rlvr_prompts:
    completion = sample(dpo, prompt)
    reward = 10 if verifier(prompt, completion) else 0
    dpo = ppo_update(dpo, reward, kl_to_ref=true)

return evaluate(dpo, evals.dev, evals.unseen)

claims.statement: Tulu 3 releases a complete open stack: model checkpoints, intermediate stages, datasets, training code, evaluation code, decontamination tooling, and a demo.
caveats: Model availability still inherits base-model licenses and infrastructure requirements.

claims.statement: The Tulu 3 recipe is multi-stage: SFT, preference tuning with length-normalized DPO, then RLVR for selected verifiable skills.
caveats: The 405B path differs from the 8B/70B recipe and uses a lighter-touch scaled setup.

claims.statement: On the paper's main evaluation suite, Tulu 3 8B and 70B outperform comparable open-weight instruct models at the same size and the 70B model matches or exceeds several smaller closed models on average.
caveats: Some closed-model scores are interpolated or sourced from model cards, and evaluation setups can differ across reports.

claims.statement: RLVR provides deterministic binary rewards for math and precise instruction-following, improving targeted test performance but not guaranteeing average performance gains across all evaluations.
caveats: RLVR is only applicable where answer extraction and verification are reliable.

claims.statement: Scaling post-training exposed concrete systems issues: loss aggregation semantics, DPO scaling cost, asynchronous RLVR inference/training, weight synchronization, and hardware restarts.
caveats: These are implementation-specific lessons, but they are exactly the sort of hidden operational detail open recipes usually omit.

claims.statement: The paper explicitly separates development and unseen evaluations and finds that some choices generalize while some instruction-following and knowledge decisions overfit development benchmarks.
caveats: For third-party models, the authors cannot verify whether their supposedly unseen tasks were used in development.

claims.statement: Several plausible training methods did not reliably improve performance, including online DPO in their setup and rejection sampling at the explored compute budget.
caveats: The paper frames these as empirical findings for the Tulu 3 setup, not universal impossibility results.

evidence.result: The release lists base, SFT, DPO, reward-model, and final checkpoints; training code in open-instruct; evaluation code in olmes; decontamination tooling; preference-data inference; SFT, preference, and RLVR datasets; and a demo.

The recipe starts from Llama 3.1 base models, curates/decontaminates data, trains SFT, runs preference tuning over on-policy data, then applies RLVR for verifiable math and instruction-following tasks.

Across explored preference-tuning algorithms on an early Tulu 3 checkpoint and UltraFeedback, only length-normalized DPO outperformed the base checkpoint overall; the best listed average score is 57.3 versus 55.7 SFT base.
RLVR samples completions, applies a deterministic verifier, gives reward alpha when correct and zero otherwise, and optimizes the policy with PPO plus KL regularization.

The main suite reports averages of 65.1 for Tulu 3 8B and 76.2 for Tulu 3 70B, compared with 62.9 for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 74.1 for Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, 69 for GPT-4o mini, 70.6 for Claude 3.5 Haiku, and 75.3 for the best closed-model column in the table.

RLVR improves targeted test performance for GSM8K, MATH, and prompts with constraints, and improves train-set verifiable rewards, but the paper states an increase in average score across all evaluations is not guaranteed.

The paper identifies mean-loss behavior under gradient accumulation and distributed training as changing sample/token weighting, and chooses sum loss with a 5e-6 learning rate and 2 epochs for SFT after experiments.
The 8B DPO model trains for about 10 hours on 8 H100s, while the 70B DPO model trains for about 19 hours on 64 interconnected H100s with maximum sequence length 2048.

RLVR uses separate GPUs for inference and training, concurrent rollout/training to reduce idle time, and weight synchronization to the inference engine, while noting stale-data and reproducibility risks.

For the 405B RLVR setup, inference uses vLLM with 16-way tensor parallelism while the remaining 240 GPUs train; inference takes about 550 seconds, weight transfer about 25 seconds, and training about 1500 seconds per iteration.

The paper builds unseen evaluations aligned to core skills, reports that final checkpoints get the best average development and unseen performance, but notes overfitting in precise instruction-following and some knowledge/reasoning choices.
The paper reports that online DPO gave little or no improvement on GSM8K and degraded MATH in their setup, and that rejection sampling produced minimal gains for the compute required.
evidence.metric: methods that did not reliably improve

agent_infra_takeaways: Open recipes need artifacts, not just weights. The reusable contribution is data, code, evals, decontamination, intermediate checkpoints, and failed-method notes.
Verifiable rewards are the agent-training hinge: when a task has an executable checker, reward generation moves from human-time to compute-time.
Evaluation should be part of the training loop from day one, with development tasks separated from unseen tasks.
Post-training is a distributed systems problem at scale: rollout engines, learner GPUs, weight sync, stale data, hardware failures, and loss semantics all affect the model.
Synthetic data is useful only with aggressive curation and contamination checks; otherwise the apparent skill may just be benchmark leakage.
Negative results are recipe data. Knowing which obvious methods failed prevents cargo-cult post-training.
caveats: The detailed PDF source used here is a v3 mirror, while the current arXiv entry is v5; the arXiv page confirms later 405B results and analyses.
The recipe is complex and resource-intensive, so reproducibility still requires substantial GPU infrastructure.
RLVR only applies cleanly where answer extraction and deterministic verification are reliable.
The paper focuses mostly on English data and evaluations, and lists long-context, multi-turn, and multilinguality as future-work areas.
Some comparisons with closed models rely on non-identical external reports, interpolated scores, or model-card numbers.
Unseen evaluations are unseen for Tulu 3, but the authors cannot verify that comparison models did not train on them.
